procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: During the preliminary hearing of this petition, Mr. Ramamurthy, representing the petitioner, raised a ground that s. 13A of the Act was ultra vires the Constitution as contravening the provisions of Art. 22 of the Constitution. That question was referred by the Constitution Bench of the Court to a larger Bench
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Petition under Article 32 of the Constitution of India presented by Sampat Prakash challenging his detention. The petitioner contended that the orders making the modifications in 1959 and 1964 could not be validly passed by the President. The grounds taken to challenge the validity of the Act fail and are rejected. The petition will now be set down for hearing arguments, if any, on the facts of the case.

directions: The petition will now be set down for hearing arguments, if any, on the facts of the case.

issue.issue_text: Whether Section 13A of the Act is ultra vires the Constitution as it contravenes the provisions of Article 22 of the Constitution.

facts: The petitioner was detained under Section 3 of the Jammu & Kashmir Preventive Detention Act, 1964.
The petitioner's detention was continued under Section 13A of the Act without a reference to an Advisory Board.
The petitioner challenged Section 13A, arguing it was unconstitutional because it violated the safeguards for preventive detention provided in Article 22 of the Constitution.
law: Article 35(c) of the Constitution, as applied to Jammu & Kashmir in 1954, protected the state's preventive detention laws from being challenged on the grounds that they violated fundamental rights (like Article 22) for a period of five years.
The President of India, acting under Article 370(1), issued orders in 1959 and 1964 that extended this protection period first to ten years, and then to fifteen years.
Article 367 of the Constitution states that the General Clauses Act, 1897, applies to the interpretation of the Constitution.
Section 21 of the General Clauses Act provides that a power to issue an order includes the power to add, amend, vary, or rescind it.
application: The petitioner's primary argument was that the five-year protection granted by Article 35(c) had expired in 1959, so the 1964 Act was not immune from a challenge based on Article 22.

The petitioner then argued that the President's orders in 1959 and 1964 extending the protection period were invalid, as the power under Article 370 could not be exercised repeatedly to amend a previous order.
The Court rejected this argument by invoking Article 367, which applies the General Clauses Act to the Constitution.

The Court applied Section 21 of the General Clauses Act to the President's power under Article 370. It reasoned that the power to issue an order applying the Constitution to J&K also includes the power to amend that order later.
Therefore, the Presidential orders extending the immunity period were a valid exercise of power.
Because the extensions were valid, Article 35(c) was in full effect when the 1964 Act was passed and when the petitioner was detained, granting the Act immunity from challenges based on Article 22.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the petitioner's challenge, holding that Section 13A of the Act could not be declared unconstitutional for contravening Article 22. This was because the Act was protected by Article 35(c) of the Constitution, which had been validly extended by Presidential orders under Article 370.

arguments.issue_text: Whether Section 13A of the Act is ultra vires the Constitution as it contravenes the provisions of Article 22 of the Constitution.
appellant_arguments: Section 13A of the Jammu & Kashmir Preventive Detention Act, 1964, is unconstitutional because it violates Article 22 of the Constitution.
The protection given to the state's preventive detention laws by Article 35(c) was initially for a limited period of five years, which has expired.
The Presidential Orders of 1959 and 1964, which extended this protection, are invalid.

These orders are invalid because Article 370, which grants the President the power to make such modifications, was intended to be a temporary provision that ceased to be effective after the Jammu & Kashmir Constituent Assembly framed the state's constitution in 1956.
The President's power under Article 370 is a constitutional power and cannot be interpreted by applying Section 21 of the General Clauses Act.
respondent_arguments: The provisions of Article 370 should be held to be continuing in force.
The historical and political situation that existed when Article 370 was incorporated into the Constitution has not materially altered.
The purpose of Article 370 was to empower the President to exercise discretion in applying the Indian Constitution while that situation remained unchanged, and therefore the power persists.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: By virtue of Article 367, which applies the General Clauses Act to the interpretation of the Constitution, the President's power to issue orders under Article 370 is a continuing power. This power includes the authority to add to, amend, vary, or rescind such orders and did not cease to be effective after the Constituent Assembly of the State passed the State's Constitution.
obiter: The possibility that when applying a particular provision, the situation might demand an exception or modification, and subsequent changes in the situation might justify the rescinding of those modifications or exceptions, is a reason for the President's power to be continuous.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The provision made in Art. 35 (c) has the effect that the validity of the Act cannot be challenged on the ground that any of the provisions of the Act are inconsistent with Art. 22 of the Constitution. The initial 1954 Presidential Order granting this immunity for five years was valid. If that initial order was not an invalid infringement of fundamental rights, then subsequent orders merely extending the period of that immunity cannot be held to be an invalid infringement or abridgement of those rights either, as the fundamental rights were already made inapplicable to the preventive detention law.
legal_tests_applied: The power to issue an order under a constitutional provision like Article 370(1)(d) includes the power to subsequently vary, alter, add to, or rescind that order, based on the rule of interpretation laid down in Section 21 of the General Clauses Act.
why_appellant_lost: The argument that Article 370 was a temporary provision that ceased to be effective after the State's Constituent Assembly framed its constitution is incorrect. The State's Constituent Assembly itself did not recommend that the article cease to be operative; instead, it recommended a modification, which implies its agreement to the continued operation of the article.

The argument that extending the period of immunity for preventive detention laws from five to fifteen years abridged fundamental rights is flawed. The fundamental rights were already made inapplicable to such laws by the original, valid order. Therefore, extending the period of their inapplicability cannot be considered an abridgement of those rights.

The court rejected the argument that Section 21 of the General Clauses Act cannot be used to interpret a constitutional power, and instead held that the President's power to 'modify' under Article 370(1)(d) includes the power to subsequently vary or alter such orders.
why_respondent_won: The court found considerable force in the submission that Article 370 should be held to be continuing in force because the historical and political situation that existed when the article was incorporated had not materially altered, and the purpose of the article was to empower the President to exercise discretion while that situation remained unchanged.

The President's power under Article 370(1)(d) to apply constitutional provisions with exceptions and modifications is an ongoing power. By applying Section 21 of the General Clauses Act, this power to issue an order includes the power to amend or vary it subsequently, thus validating the 1959 and 1964 orders that extended the immunity period.

The effect of Article 35(c) was not to abridge a fundamental right, but rather to postpone the applicability of Part III of the Constitution for the purpose of judging the validity of a state preventive detention law. The subsequent orders merely extended this period of postponement.
policy_considerations: The provisions of Art. 370 should be held to be continuing in force, because the situation that existed when this article was incorporated in the Constitution had not materially altered, and the purpose of introducing this article was to empower the President to exercise his discretion in applying the Indian Constitution while that situation remained unchanged.
